avoid anything that could be stressful

Threat.value: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.item: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: 'Never Alone' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of police violence and the rest of the profile. This item more strongly suggests fear of being alone with a potentially abusive intimate or familiar person, whereas the threat items center on strangers and general vigilance. That mismatch is difficult to explain clinically within the same trauma-linked profile.

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Contamination' is not well aligned with the trauma type and accompanying appraisals. Feeling dirty or contaminated is more characteristic of sexual trauma; with police violence, and with the current memory/threat content, this appraisal stands out as clinically incongruent rather than merely unusual.

vignette: John, a 58-year-old dentist of North American ethnicity, experienced a traumatic event involving police violence that has left him with significant PTSD symptoms. The incident occurred several months ago when John was leaving his dental clinic late one night. He had been pulled over by police officers who mistook the tools in his car for illegal activity. During the encounter, he was aggressively questioned and physically restrained, despite his repeated assurances of his innocence. Since that night, John’s life has changed drastically. He now avoids any situation where he might experience negative or positive feelings, fearing they might lead to a resurgence of traumatic memories or intense emotions. This avoidance extends to all aspects of his daily routine, including social interactions and even professional activities at the dental clinic. His aversion to stressors means that he often declines invitations from colleagues and clients alike, isolating himself both professionally and personally. John’s constant scanning of his surroundings for signs of threat has become a relentless habit, affecting how he navigates everyday situations. He is particularly wary of strangers approaching him, feeling threatened even in ordinary settings such as grocery stores or at the dentist’s office where patients might come too close to him. This hyper-vigilance often leads to moments of intense anxiety and fear, especially when he feels cornered or unable to escape quickly. The memory of that traumatic night still haunts John in vivid detail. When these memories return, they feel alien as if they belonged to someone else, rather than an experience he lived through. He sometimes hears the voices of the police officers questioning him and feels the physical pain where he was restrained. These intrusive recollections disrupt his ability to focus on his work and personal life, often leaving him feeling detached from reality. John’s negative appraisals have deeply affected how he views himself and his future. He believes there is something inherently wrong with him that made the event happen, and this sense of fault has compounded his feelings of injustice and loss. The trauma feels like a shattering blow to his life, destroying what once was familiar and comfortable. Despite his best efforts to move forward, John remains preoccupied by thoughts of how unfair it all seems, and he harbors no hope that anything can be done about the situation. John’s avoidance behaviors have led to significant consequences in both his professional and personal life. His dental practice has seen a decline as he avoids interacting with patients and colleagues, leading to strained relationships within the clinic. At home, John’s partner notices a growing distance between them as he withdraws from shared activities and social outings. These changes have created tension and misunderstanding in their relationship. What finally brought John to seek help was his increasing inability to function at work and the realization that his isolation was taking a toll on both his mental health and relationships. He is most afraid of losing control completely, feeling overwhelmed by the constant fear and pain associated with his memories. At the same time, he hopes for some relief from the relentless anxiety and a chance to reclaim parts of his life that have been lost to trauma. Through therapy, John aims to understand how his experiences have shaped his current fears and behaviors, and to develop strategies to manage his symptoms more effectively. He is determined to find a way back to a sense of normalcy and peace, despite the significant obstacles he faces.
